title: Majukayong Tribe [cite: 61]
location: Maducayan and Saliok, Natonin, Mt. Province [cite: 62]
summary_statement: Fierce guardians of ancestral melodies who transformed a history of headhunting into a vibrant, peaceful musical identity. [cite: 64]
full_content: The Majukayong tribe resides in the barangays of Maducayan and Saliok, where their traditions and dialect remain closely related to the Kalinga. [cite: 65]
Historically known for their bravery and protective nature, they have long since transitioned from ancient headhunting practices to a culture rooted in peace and ancestral remembrance. [cite: 66]
Music and dance are the heart of their communal occasions, honoring their ancestors and passing the soul of the tribe on to younger generations. [cite: 67]
Like their neighbors, they remain cautious with their traditional knowledge, treating it with the respect it deserves. [cite: 68]
The Majukayong musical repertoire is deeply functional and tied to specific rites. [cite: 69]
The Ayég Udén is a bamboo rainmaker filled with pebbles or seeds, used exclusively by tribe elders to call for rain. [cite: 70]
For courtship and marriage rites such as the Bérogwey, they play the Jungajung (stomping tubes) and the Patangguk (quill-shaped percussion tubes). [cite: 71]
The Patangguk is particularly significant — played by men visiting the house of a future bride, and sounded at night to ward off bad omens. [cite: 72]
Their music is not mere entertainment; it is a spiritual shield and a communal bond. [cite: 73]
Their craftsmanship relies heavily on Schizostachyum lumampao (known locally as Vuru) and Gigantochloa levis (Béyog). [cite: 74]
For instruments like the Béllingving (buzzers), they adjust pitch using the tuknor, a woven rattan ring that acts as a capo. [cite: 75]
The Tabbatab zither ensemble is especially complex, featuring either two strings over a bamboo plate or a single string across a resonant tube. [cite: 76]
These instruments are carefully air-dried for at least a week, with the nodes perforated for wind instruments like the Bérédong so the player's breath can flow freely through the wood. [cite: 77]

quote.text: "Our music makes our occasions lively and keeps the memory of our ancestors alive in every beat." [cite: 78]
